title: Crock-Pot Jollof Rice
author: Fran Osseo-Asare
desc: An experiment she published with its verdict attached — right flavour, tender meat, and very mushy rice with some grains undercooked.
longDesc: This is a failed experiment published honestly, which makes it more useful than most successes. A slow cooker is preheated on high about thirty minutes, everything goes in including raw rice, and it cooks an hour on high then about seven more on low. Her verdict on the beef version is printed in full: right flavour, tender meat, but very mushy rice with some grains undercooked. The vegetarian version was better, needing less tomato paste and about six hours. Her conclusion is that the oven is her first choice and the stovetop second — and that a commenter's advice was simply not to make jollof in a crock-pot at all.
ingredients: 1 lb stewing beef, such as chuck
Well-drained tomatoes, seeded if you wish, from a 28 oz tin — about a cup
3 tbsp peanut or other vegetable oil
1 whole chilli pepper, seeded — or about 1/2 tsp red pepper flakes
1 tsp curry powder, thyme or other herb (optional)
2 tsp seasoning salt, or regular salt, or to taste
Parchment paper, tapped over the rice
steps: Preheat the crock-pot on high for about 30 minutes.
Add the broth, tomato juice, drained tomatoes, beef, oil, onion, ginger, tomato paste, garlic, chilli, pepper, herb, salt and bay leaf.
Add the raw rice — it is not parboiled.
Cook on high for an hour.
Reduce the heat to low and cook for about 7 more hours.
Add the chopped vegetables about an hour before serving.
// For the vegetarian version: use only 1 to 1 1/2 tablespoons of tomato paste and cook about 6 hours.
Tap a sheet of parchment over the rice — not taped — in place of plastic wrap.
chefTips: Read her verdict before you commit eight hours: right flavour, tender meat, but very mushy rice with some grains undercooked. She published the experiment and its result together.
The vegetarian version was the better of the two, with less tomato paste and about six hours rather than eight.
Parchment tapped — not taped — over the rice, which she substituted for plastic wrap. It is the slow-cooker equivalent of the foil-under-the-lid trick.
Her ranking is explicit: the oven is her first choice, the stovetop second. The crock-pot is third and she says so.
A commenter's verdict, quoted on the page and worth knowing: they still do not recommend making jollof in a crock-pot because it is too soft.
Preheat the crock-pot thirty minutes before anything goes in. Cold ceramic plus raw rice is part of why the grains cook unevenly.
A practice she reports from Ghana explains the parchment: cooks there often put plastic wrap over covered rice even with a lid on, apparently to help it steam.
commonMistakes: Expecting non-mushy rice from this method.
Using the beef version's tomato paste quantity in the vegetarian one.
Taping rather than tapping the parchment down.
Adding the vegetables at the start of eight hours.
sources: Adapted from three consecutive posts on betumiblog.blogspot.com dated 22-23 October 2009: 'Recipe-in-progress: crockpot jollof rice'; 'Crockpot jollof rice revisited'; and 'Recipe #25: Jollof rice in a crock pot'. BYLINE AS PRINTED on all three: 'Posted by Fran'. The Recipe #25 post is timestamped 12:42 PM, 23 October 2009 and labelled 'crockpot jollof rice, vegetarian jollof'; it is narrative with NO ingredient list.

Beef version ingredients, exactly as printed and TWO-PASS consistent: 1 cup broth; 1 cup tomato juice or water; well drained tomatoes (seeded, if you wish), from a 28 oz. can of tomatoes (plum, if possible) (about a cup); 1 pound of stewing beef (such as chuck); 3 tablespoons peanut or other vegetable oil; 2 cups of onion, chopped (about 2 medium); 1 tablespoon of fresh peeled ginger, chopped; 1/3 cup tomato paste (5 tablespoons); 4 cloves of garlic, minced; 1/2 teaspoon black or white pepper (optional); 1 whole chili pepper, seeded (or substitute about 1/2 teaspoon red pepper flakes); 1 teaspoon curry powder, thyme, or other herb (optional); 2 teaspoons seasoning (like Adobo) or regular salt, or to taste; 1 bay leaf (optional); 2 cups chopped vegetables; 1 1/2 cups of long grain rice.

Method as printed: preheat the crockpot on high 'for about 30 minutes'; 'Cook on high for an hour, then reduce the heat to low and cook for about 7 more hours'; add vegetables about an hour before serving. THE RICE GOES IN RAW, with no parboiling.
THE 'REVISITED' POST is SINGLE-PASS and gave only fragments: '1 cup of rice', '1/2 cup of tomato juice from the can', '2 tablespoons of peanut oil', and 'put it on... to cook on high'.
THE AUTHOR'S OWN VERDICT, verbatim and the reason this entry exists: 'right flavor, tender meat, but, yuk, very mushy rice, with some grains undercooked'.

A COMMENTER'S VERDICT, quoted on the page: 'I still don't recommend making your jollof in a crockpot--it's too soft'. ATTRIBUTION CAVEAT: that this came from a commenter rather than the author is SINGLE-PASS and unverified.

RECIPE #25, TWO-PASS: the vegetarian version was better; tomato paste 'maybe 1 to 1 1/2 Tablespoons'; cook time 'a little less--maybe six hours'; the oven is 'my first choice' and the stovetop second; and parchment tapped '(NOT taped)' over the rice, replacing plastic wrap.

A PRACTICE SHE REPORTS FROM GHANA, SINGLE-PASS and quoted: 'In Ghana they often put a piece of plastic wrap over the covered rice while it is cooking, even though they have a lid on the pot. My guess is that it's to somehow help the rice steam.' NOTE that this collection's Nigerian party jollof uses a double layer of foil or parchment under the lid for exactly that purpose, which corroborates her guess.
NO DONENESS CUE is given for the crock-pot versions beyond the times.

WHY A FAILED EXPERIMENT IS PUBLISHED: it is documented, named, quantified, and carries its own honest verdict, which makes it genuinely informative about what the dish needs. Her ranking of oven over stovetop over slow cooker is the practical conclusion of three published attempts.
NO YIELD is printed. The six servings above is an editorial reading of 1½ cups of rice.
reheating: Steam, or microwave with a splash of water.
healthBenefits: Long slow cooking makes the beef's collagen and minerals more available.
High in lycopene from the tomato.
Vegetarian as the author's better version.
culturalNote: A cook publishing an eight-hour experiment along with the word 'yuk' is doing something more valuable than publishing a success — it tells you that jollof's texture depends on even, controllable heat, which is exactly why her oven method works and this one does not.
